subject: 🏷️ Repricing the AI trade
body_text:
96 
Plus: Boss AI | Wednesday, October 21, 2026
   
 
 View in browser 
   
 
 Presented By Barclays Investment Bank 
   
 Axios Markets By
Emily Peck and Matt Phillips
 · 
Oct 21, 2026
 
 
 🤩 Wednesday! How exuberant are we? That's the key question about the AI trade this week. This morning, the optimists have an edge.

 S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures are higher after SpaceX reported eye-popping increases in AI revenue and disclosed that its board and Tesla's had formed committees exploring a tie-up of the two Elon Musk companies, which would create an AI-centered colossus. Anthropic may spend $750 billion on computing in the coming years, says the Wall Street Journal , citing a draft IPO prospectus. Next test: Meta reports earnings after the close. 🧐 Plenty of other signs show the AI trade entering an era of modified exuberance. Emily explains below. 

 Plus, a new survey finds executives are more likely than employees to trust AI over their own judgment, which is what they get paid for, right? Don't tarry! 1,079 words, a 4-minute read. 


 
   
   
 
1 big thing: The AI trade gets a reappraisal
 
 By Emily Peck 
   
 
 
 
 Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Stock: Getty Images


 
   
 
 The AI boom is moving into its rational exuberance phase, to adapt a term from the last tech bubble: Investors are pulling back funding and demanding more evidence that their investments will actually pay off.

 Why it matters: It's a delicate dance. The economy is running on the AI trade right now. Can investors take air out of the bubble without popping the whole damn thing? 

 The big picture: Investors still believe that long-term AI will pay off in big productivity gains — and that's clear from the gains in the stock market — but lately they've toned down the mania.

 Signs of the retreat are coming from all corners of the AI buildout: Neoclouds are the hardest hit. These are the new players borrowing heavily and using backing from Big Tech companies to build data centers and sell computing power back to those hyperscalers, as part of what many see as the AI circular economy. 

 Bond investors are demanding more compensation to lend to neoclouds — CoreWeave is Exhibit A — as rising interest rates make them look more risky. South Korean neocloud Elice's stock plunged more than 30% in its trading debut yesterday. In Australia, an Nvidia-backed neocloud called Firmus shelved a planned IPO earlier this month after investors balked at its valuation. "We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation," said John Pearce, the chief investment officer of one of Australia's largest pension funds, in explaining why his fund wouldn't participate in the stock offering. The latest: Nvidia might be poised to swoop in and invest hundreds of millions in Firmus, the Information reports. The deep-pocketed chipmaking behemoth is already an investor, and a big backer of neoclouds.

 Chipmakers are also getting a reappraisal. Since the tech-heavy Nasdaq peaked at an all-time high on Oct. 6, chip stocks have slid.

 Even Big Tech is getting a second look. The hyperscalers like Amazon, Meta and Google parent Alphabet began the AI boom using their enormous cash stockpiles to build data centers.

 Now, these giants have moved on to borrowing — a lot. And investors are adjusting. "They started by financing with free cash flow. That kind of ran out," David Lebovitz, head of alternative research and strategy at JPMorgan Asset Management, said at an event Monday. "Now, they're moving into the credit markets. Well, credit markets are having a little bit of an indigestion period." Data: FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips Yes, but: For now, Wall Street is holding on to the belief that AI will transform markets and the economy. 

 Take JPMorgan. On Monday, the bank raised its forecast for annual returns on U.S. large-cap stocks to 7.5% over the next 10 to 15 years, up from 6.7% last year — courtesy of AI-driven productivity gains and resilient corporate profit margins. And even the boom's most prominent skeptics concede that a massive transformation is happening. The bursting of the dot-com bubble didn't mean the internet went away. Zoom out: "My point was that we have had this blind enthusiasm for all things AI – endless financing, companies converting business models and a relentless focus on building as much computing power as possible," JPMorgan's Lebovitz later told Axios. 

 "What you are seeing now is that markets are beginning to differentiate between players, business models and financing approaches." The bottom line: It's becoming clear that AI is no Lake Wobegon, where all the companies are above average and good-looking.

2. Executives: In AI we trust 
 
 By Emily Peck 
   
 
 
 
 Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images


 
   
 
 Executives are twice as likely as rank-and-file workers to trust AI over their own judgment, per a survey out this morning.

 Why it matters: It's a worrying development. Leaders are hired for their experience and knowledge. 

 Outsourcing that to AI raises the risk of making decisions that don't line up with reality, which then reverberate across companies and beyond. By the numbers: 32.8% of executives said that they trust AI more than their own judgment, according to the survey from Charter, a workplace research and media company.

 That's twice the rate for workers, or individual contributors. Just 16.3% of individual contributors said the same. Zoom out: "Cognitive offloading" is a term for using tools like AI to reduce mental effort. 

 "Executives—despite having the most experience—are doing it more than anyone," the report's coauthors wrote. By the numbers: Charter surveyed 5,002 U.S. office workers at companies with at least 100 employees who said they use AI at work, including 2,952 individual contributors, 1,547 managers and 503 executives — including vice presidents, C-suite executives, owners and founders.

 Between the lines: Most executives are under a lot of pressure to know the answers to a lot of questions really quickly — and AI can help with that at least in the short term, says Brian Elliott, a former Slack executive who is now executive-in-residence at Charter and cowrote the report.

 AI "lends itself very well to the 'seldom wrong, never in doubt' tendency that some executives have," he says. "If you feel like you have to fake it until you make it as an executive, then AI is certainly going to feed those tendencies because you can appear to be really smart, really quick." Reality check: The Charter survey measures executives' self-reported trust in AI, but not whether they actually follow its advice when making consequential decisions.

 The report's findings were overall positive about AI's potential in the workplace. 42.7% of AI users said it improved both their work and personal lives.
